paragraphs.heading: Do they believe Jesus is God?
paragraphs.edited: When you're talking to your students about Jesus, do you automatically assume that they believe Jesus to be God? For years I did. I just assumed it, until I got into a conversation with them about it and realized that that's not always the case. Not that long ago, I was talking with a couple of young guys who came to my door. They were Mormons.

paragraphs.heading: Who Jesus claims to be
paragraphs.edited: So it's very possible that even in your context, when you talk about Jesus, you may be talking on a different plane than some of your students are. But this is a great opportunity to be crystal clear on exactly who it is that Jesus actually is, and who he says he is. That's why we have students focus right in on John 8, because it's here that Jesus makes the flat-out statement, "Before Abraham was born, I am." The focus here is who Jesus claims to be.

paragraphs.heading: The intro activity
paragraphs.edited: So we ask students in the intro activity to put down who they think they are, what their family and friends would say about them, and then whether that matches up. And do they have evidence for this? They think they're somebody — they think they're a soccer player, or a Christian, or a musician, or a football player, or whatever. Do they have evidence for it? I used to call myself a football player because I played football, but a person once brought it up to me and said, "You don't really play football." I said, "Well, what do you mean?" He said, "Well, you sit the bench." So was I really a football player? Probably not so much. So who do they think they are, and what evidence do they have for it?

paragraphs.heading: Just a good moral teacher
paragraphs.edited: In your small group time, one thing that I bet is probably going to come out — and you'll want to make sure your small group leaders are ready to deal with it — is this: it's not hard, I don't think, to look at Jesus as a great moral teacher, as someone who has this wonderful religious sage kind of vibe going on, where they can read what he says about love and forgiveness and acceptance and mercy and justice and all these great things that Jesus talks about, like in the Sermon on the Mount, and leave it there.

paragraphs.heading: What I saw in my students
paragraphs.edited: So believe it or not, one thing that I found among some of my students back when I was teaching was that a lot of students really loved Jesus and really liked what he taught, but had very little to no intention of ever following him as God. And that bothered me. It was right there. It was under my nose, and half the time I don't even know if I noticed it. But after a while it became very apparent, once I started looking for it. So it changed the way I taught, and it changed the way I started to converse with some of my students, and I started to challenge them.

paragraphs.heading: Who do you say I am?
paragraphs.edited: And I think small group, in this time and in this lesson, might be a perfect opportunity for you to challenge your students with this question: how do you see Jesus? It's similar to how Jesus addressed Peter in Matthew chapter 16 — "Who do you say I am?" Ask your students, who do you say Jesus is? And when they answer you, whatever their answer is, ask them why. Get some answers out of them as to why they think that.

paragraphs.edited: And if they're in that place where Jesus is just a good moral teacher, ask them what it would take to get them to see him as God. Is there enough evidence? I mean, you've presented the evidence, and there's a whole bunch of it. If you look through all the verses, we've only given you a spattering of the verses that show that Jesus is God. So what does that mean for them? Is there not enough evidence, or are they just not willing? It can be an eye-opening experience.
